Ravid Shwartz-Ziv: Hey, everyone, and welcome back to the Information, uh, Bottleneck Podcast. And today we have Zhuang Liu. He's a assistant professor, uh, at Princeton. Hi, Zhuang. Nice to have you.

Zhuang Liu: Hi, Ravid. Mm. Hi, Alan. Mm-hmm.

Ravid Shwartz-Ziv: And as always, we have Alan. Hey, Alan.

Allen Roush: It's good to see you again, Ravid. Nice to meet you, Zhuang. And, uh, yeah, you should go take a look at his Google Scholar. He has a lot of really cool papers.

Ravid Shwartz-Ziv: Yeah, so we'll talk about some of these papers, uh, today. And in general, we are going to talk about what are the important components, uh, in today AIs. Okay? So you have so, Zhuang, you have so many works. Uh, I think we can start with some understanding of what do you think are the important component. So, uh, a few years ago, you had a paper about, uh, a conv, a convnet for the 2020s, right?

Zhuang Liu: Mm-hmm.

Ravid Shwartz-Ziv: Um, that, you know what? Maybe you'll tell us about what is the, the paper about, and then we can start to, to start to decompose the-

Zhuang Liu: Mm-hmm

Ravid Shwartz-Ziv: ... the components for current, uh, AI systems.

Zhuang Liu: Mm-hmm. Yes, of course. So that was a really interesting story. So the paper, we, we were working on this paper in twen- 2021, and back then, transformers has just entered the computer vision's, world, computer vision research space, through the introduction of vision transformers, right? And then everybody from the vision community have, have been, switching to vision transformers from more traditional convnets, and they are getting better and better performance. So in, so in this work, we want to say, we want to investigate, whether truly, like, convnet is, has lost its, competitiveness, and whether it's possible to, to, control all the design components there is to study whether convnets can be modernized to be, on par with vision transformers at that time.

So we wanna study whether it's a, it's a difference that seeming, seemingly, performance gap between transform- vision transformers and convnets is due to their inherent design, like whether you use self-attention or convolution or due to other small, like seemingly small design details. So, and we found the answer to be, the latter. So after a lot of studying, in, of like modernizing the design compon- components of a convnet, we eventually get the model to be on par with, vision transformers, very strong vision transformers at that time on a diverse range of tasks. So this demonstrates that, no matter you choose convnet or vision transformers, as long as you get the des- the, everything correct, you'll, you'll get, the same frontier level performance on vision tasks.

Yeah.

Ravid Shwartz-Ziv: And do you still believe that this is true? Do you still believe that like at the end, it doesn't really matter?

Zhuang Liu: I wouldn't s-- Yeah, I, I largely tend to agree, but I wou- I wouldn't say it doesn't matter. it's, I, I would say, as long as you get everything correct, like as long as you have, y- explore the s- the design space enough, you'll converge to some point where it's like kind of the Pareto frontier in terms of accuracy and efficiency trade-off. And it's very hard to go off this frontier. like I think in the past, many years, there haven't been real- really, like innovations that, have been widely adopted other than the, kind of the mature architectures that we, we already were working with, several years ago. but, but this process itself is very, very fun. in fact, recently there have been some, paper releases on this, especially from this, open, open weight model companies like Kimi, DeepSeek.

They're still playing around with architectures, like how do you, how do you change residual connections? How do you, connect different layers? these kind of stuff. And, and I respect that work a lot. In fact, part of the reason that architecture research is less active in academia right now is that, we couldn't really afford to, afford the compute to demonstrate these effects in, in, convincing scale. So that's a, a sad part, but I still try to play around with it myself using our, resources at, at, university. actually, with the help of Cloud Code, I can now, go back to coding to, to play around in the first hand myself. So this is very fun research, but in, I do think in, from a practical stand, point of view, what data we learn, what data we train the model on matters more than, the architecture choice.

As long as the interface, the input/output interface stays the same, architecture, architecture is how we parameterize the function approximator, right? The, the very basic function of, of neural networks or deep learning. And how we parameterize it, no matter, as long as you get like a few things correct, like using residual connections, using self-attention or, or other like, reasonable mechanisms, and having the right activation at the right places, feed forward, layers at the right places, you'll be at the f- very close or at the frontier, curve of this, performance, versus efficiency, balance. And, then I was, I, I would tend to think that what, what matters more in terms of practical usage, in terms of bringing the product to more and more people to be more effective in their daily usage.

I do think other, other aspects like what data has this model been trained on, how it can handle context and memory is what, what matters more. So in terms of context and memory, yes, there are-- there do exist architectural work that, address that. So I think that is kind of the more immediate problems we, we need to address in, in making AI like up another level. Yeah.

Allen Roush: In a ConvNet for the 2020s, uh, first of all, you know, maybe just give your summary of that paper, but, but then my, my question is, um, you know, as I read it, uh, it looks like you, you gr-- and also correct me if this, uh, uh, my understanding is wrong, but my understanding is you gradually modernize ResNet towards a Swin-like design and end up-

Zhuang Liu: Right

Allen Roush: ... with a ConvNet that competes strongly with transformers. Um, which single ablation did you, like in that paper, most changed your own mind about where the supposed transformer advantage was really coming from?

Zhuang Liu: what ablation? I think it's every ablation. If you, if you look at the graph, nothing single-handedly, transformed, like brought, brought up the performance by large margin. Like some of them are more useful than others, but, it's not really that one change changed everything. maybe the, I, I guess the use of activation and norm-- redu-reduction of normalization layers is one thing that, kind of intrigued me and, has a noticeable performance change. but it was really everything together. So these seemingly small components, when we compound them together, they can, they can really cause large differences that would normally attribute to, some, some substantial change, like changing convolution to a self-attention or in, into, modernized, say, more modern mechanisms like linear attention, right?

So, so I think the, the big lesson here is, these small details when combined together matters much more than the sim- seemingly core components of the networks. Yeah.

Ravid Shwartz-Ziv: But do you think it's-- because for me, it looks that like we have, like we are trying a lot of things. Some of these things are working, right?

Zhuang Liu: Mm-hmm.

Ravid Shwartz-Ziv: And then we get better models.

Zhuang Liu: Mm-hmm.

Ravid Shwartz-Ziv: And then like in retrospective, like we can, we can start like to understand like exactly what the component that are actually matter, right? Like we can-

Zhuang Liu: Mm-hmm

Ravid Shwartz-Ziv: ... try to, oh, so now let's change ConvNet and, and make it look, looks more as a, as a transformer, for example, right?

Zhuang Liu: Mm-hmm.

Ravid Shwartz-Ziv: Um, do you agree with that? Do you think that like this is something that we actually need, need this breakthrough, and then we can trace back and, uh, understand the, the details and try to match other methods? Or do you think like we just need to try again and again, and, uh, we don't need the very specific, uh, directions?

Zhuang Liu: I see. Got it. Yeah, I think transformer absolutely is a blessing to the, to the community and also the vision transformers, the, the adoption of transformers in computer vision. I don't debate that. That's, that's hard to debate. it's, it's absolutely a breakthrough, a very important breakthrough. perh- perhaps the, the biggest breakthrough in, in that, years. and, so our study was more focusing on like computer vision only domains. But another benefit of vision transformers is that they, they allow the unification of, of text and image representations, right? it's, it's then the use of transformer is very important for later developments like, LLaVA, like this multimodal framework where you have text enc-- vision encoders encode the vision into tokens, and then just treat tokens, get them together to be fed into a, a downstream LLMs.

It's a basic framework of a lot of multimodal models right now. So I think, the adoption of transformers in vision is v- a big stamp, big step for unification of multimodal data. This is, back to the, our study. Investigation of details, I, I would say it's more of a lesson. It's l- not, I think it changed my understanding more than, more than like... I'm, I'm more proud of this work because it changes my own understanding and some other, a lot of other people's understanding rather than like we now can go really, like you can still stay with ConvNets. I, I-- people can still do that. The ConvNets has its own benefits as well, especially when, restricted to computer vision only.

It's, it's convenient to deploy. It's, kind of easier to understand, especially it, may also have, better support for higher resolution long con-- long, long sequences because the operation is local. I, I, I think they just excel at different places. and this, this study-... transformation of details is a, a, is more kind of a lesson for me rather than like, we need to figure out each component, how, how much they contributes to, to performance, difference. Yeah.

Ravid Shwartz-Ziv: So, okay. So these are, uh, okay, so, so architecture is not so important, and you also like you have a more recent paper that you actually showed that, uh, uh, normalization layers are not so important, right? That you can basically can, um, remove normalization layer using, uh, um, uh, a tangent, uh, um, activation function, right? And, and maybe you need to do, uh, some tweak and, and to, to, to treat it a bit differently, but-

Zhuang Liu: Mm-hmm

Ravid Shwartz-Ziv: ... it works fine.

Zhuang Liu: Mm-hmm. Mm-hmm.

Ravid Shwartz-Ziv: So what do you think is the, what do you think are the important components and, you know, the core components that you say like, okay, these are so important for AI, for deep learning, and, and why Only in the recent years, like we, we came up with such good models. Well, why-- if, if architecture, um, doesn't matter, why we only have good AI models in the last, like, five years or 10?

Zhuang Liu: Yeah. it's a good question. Yeah. so first, transformers was brought up into the world 10 years ago, nine years ago. so it was a long time before. And even after that, we, we still follow like a similar fundamental framework right now with, with some minor changes like activation layers, mix of expert, mixture of experts that's not always needed, and also some change on how, like local attention, sliding window attentions. But the same, frameworks is still the same as, nine years ago when the paper initially came out. So I think that's the answer to that would be, for me, it would be just the s- the data, the scale of data we train them on, the scale of compute we use to train them. like, like it's, it's, like the, the classic story from GPT-1 to GPT-3, right?

Once you try and train the model, train the basically the same model using more compute, more data, more diverse data, more, internet scale data, we all get this emerging very competitive, performance we, we see now. So I would attribute that to, to, to, to the data and, and also secondarily to the, to the compute, to the how, how, how many, epochs we train on the same data. I think, I think actually, it's mostly data because now we train most models with less or just equal around, around one epoch. Yeah.

Allen Roush: I, I, I see that this thesis permeate through your work about, uh, the field is confounding architecture with recipe, right?

Zhuang Liu: Mm-hmm.

Allen Roush: Specifically in your ConvNext paper, um, right? If you were setting rules for like architecture papers today, and maybe you do these exact rules for your students-

Zhuang Liu: Mm-hmm

Allen Roush: ... what controls would you require, right, before someone can claim that some inductive bias-

Zhuang Liu: Okay

Allen Roush: ... some, especially like a new one matters?

Zhuang Liu: Got this. ideal, in ideal world, we would have unlimited compute, right? So, so first of all, I would require, I would require the effect, the benefit to be demonstrated on a, on a state-of-art scale, like, like, not necessarily frontier models, but like 7B, 30B. Yeah, but, I think scale is, is important for industry to really, see the benefit, to be convinced about the, the change, the benefits. But that's not always possible, so I wouldn't-- it's just, in ideal world. But secondly, if you want to study these mechanisms, architecture changes in smaller scales, like the ones we could do in, reasonable resource, with reason- reasonable resources, I would s- I would require first, hyperparameter sweep. we need to-- we, we, we cannot, demonstrate the, the new architecture just on one set of-- it works on one set of hyperparameters better, than the old model, especially when that hyperparameter is tuned just, just for that model. so ideally every-- so each model should compare against each other on their own best hyperparameter settings.

And the most important hyperparameters would be learning rate, weight decay, optimizers with the optimi- optimizers, optimizer types. And, it just bothers me a lot when people re- don't even tune the learning rate and, and then claim like-- people only tune the learning rate of their own method without tuning the learning rate of the baseline. That's kind of the, the easiest, like most, common fix for a lot of, claims that, that, turn out not to be generalizing. that's for one. And secondly, I would require the, the idea or the method to be demonstrated on more than one dataset, especially on, it should be on reasonable scale dataset. I would say ImageNet is still applicable today, but ideally they should also demonstrate the idea to work on, some, some small scale large language models, say for, for example, training on FineWeb.

But I understand that not every lab has the resource to do that. But I, I, I'm a big fan of like demonstrating ideas on a diverse range of datasets, at least the common datasets like people, people work on. so I guess that's, the two standards I would, I would impose. Yeah.

Ravid Shwartz-Ziv: Do you think-- I have a question. Do you think like this is some like, Anton, if, if, if you have a good idea-

Zhuang Liu: Mm-hmm

Ravid Shwartz-Ziv: ... it should work on different domains, different datasets, different, uh, uh, places? Um, or like there are very good ideas that actually work on very specific, uh, scenarios.

Zhuang Liu: Mm-hmm. Right. Right. I s- I do think, both are, both are equally valuable. in second case, so I would, want to know what specific, how to describe that specific scenario that the model works better. and there still should be more than one dataset. if you claim that your model works on like long context, long, audios, you can still like do, do, do multiple datasets on that, and, and give an explanation of why the model, the method is good on this particular, domain, right? yeah, and then we can, can start from there and see, address the weaknesses of why it doesn't work on other domains and, and go from there. or, or maybe we are good with the fact that it, it only works on this domain, and we can just, like to try to increase that gap.

So I do think both are valuable. I'm not, I'm not-- So that's a value of research, right? We, we-- You are given a... You are not required to be all successful at the, at the first step. Yeah. Though that would be good, but it's not a necessi-necessity. Yeah.

Ravid Shwartz-Ziv: And so l-let's talk a bit about data, okay? You said that this is like the important part here. Um, what exactly in the data? Uh, right, maybe le-let's start with talking about your, uh, uh, your paper. I think it was like, I don't know, several months ago, right? A year ago, about, uh, decades, uh, battles on-

Zhuang Liu: Mm-hmm

Ravid Shwartz-Ziv: ... datasets bias. So let's start, uh, describe or like explain us what does it mean, what you have tried, what was the motivation to-

Zhuang Liu: Mm-hmm

Ravid Shwartz-Ziv: ... to try, uh, to revisit some, uh, old, uh, battles?

Zhuang Liu: Yep. so I will first talk a little bit about the context, the background. so over years, people have been-- So this, this, this paper is more vision-focused. over years, people have been developing larger and larger datasets and, from more and more diverse sources. For example, initially we had MNIST, and then CIFAR, and then ImageNet, and then this internet scale datasets like, DataCamp or, Conceptual Captions, CC, dataset from Google. And they have more and more, seemingly more and more diverse images, and they are larger and larger to the billion, from, from like, tens of thousands to billion scale. And, it's, it's, it was kind of tempting to make the assumption that we are good, already good with datasets because it's really all the things you can get from internet, from these datasets. but in some of our initial experiments, we found that these datasets are nothing, still nothing like each other.

And how, how do we measure this? We, we designed a very dumb experiment that's, doesn't make sense at all as a, as a, like, a deep learning training, program. What we did is this. given three very large scale computer vision datasets, we train and classify neural network to classify, to classify which, which dataset a given particular image comes from. It's not a practical problem, it's just to try to guess the dataset's origin. it's a multi-ca- multiclass classification problem. It turns out, even with these seemingly non-- very diverse datasets, the model can still tell this answer with surprisingly high accuracy, up to, more, higher than 80% accuracy when, when you have three datasets.

So the random guessing accuracy will be 33%, but in fact, the model can be, much better, than that. So this say, this means to a model, these datasets still, are still very, very different. It has very clear cues for the model to tell which dataset this, this image comes from. Of course, we are doing this on held out validation sets. We are not, like, predicting the training, training images. but still, this has been surprisingly high, surprisingly accurate, and, that like prompts us to reflect, are we really su- have we, we really been successful in curating a large scale, all-encompassing dataset, at least in computer vision domain? What, and what, what kind of dataset is the end goal?

It's kind of hard to define this so-called all-encompassing global distribution dataset. Different people might have different criterion, and it might not be a reasonable assumption there. So should we-- So because, a big story of the success of LM is that it can do-- It's not a, like, domain-specific, specific model, right? So we want the model to be able to do everything, and in order for that to happen, we need a model,... a common assumption is that we need the model to, to have seen everything during training. And how, how, how, how much progress are we making on that? It seems from this initial experiment that we, we haven't, reached that point, yet, and still makes sense to think about how do we curate these datasets for, for the model to be really generalizing, to, to every task we want the model to be good at.

Yeah.

Ravid Shwartz-Ziv: So w-what is the answer, do you think? Like, what do you think we actually need from a good data? What types of properties-

Zhuang Liu: Mm-hmm

Ravid Shwartz-Ziv: ... I know, diversity, some uncertainty, an uncertainty, um, redundancy. What, what do you think we actually need from good, uh, data?

Zhuang Liu: Mm-hmm. Yeah, I would say, yes, diversity of content, diversity of styles, diversity of... I think it depends on-- I think a big lesson of deep learning is that, what you-- If you want the model to be good at something, you better train it at something. and, if you want to be good at everything, you need to train at everything. but, but in, in today's regime, we still mi- have this trade-off problem, right? It's we, we don't have unlimited compute, although we have built this giant data center, we still have limited compute, limited capacity of the model. So the different, capabilities of the model have learned may, may still compete with each other. meaning that if you want the model to be better at code, coding, it might, you, you might need to sacrifice a little bit on the model's, say, like, psychological counseling abilities for, for users, right?

Just, that's just an example. and how would we ba- want to balance, how do we develop a mixture of training data with the right, con- representation and with enough representation for each, each thing we want the model to, to be good at, and to be good enough at? That's kind of the how to, how to balance different domains of data, is kind of, important design. And what we found actually, um- In our recent project of text-to-image generation, we actually found a surprisingly simple solution for-- it's, it's not the best, but it's simple enough, which is to get all the good set-- get-- divide all the domains you care about. Roughly divide-- have the domain to be equal importance to each other.

You don't want to have, say, like how to, how to do haircut equally represented as how to do coding, right? They are like of different importance to, to most people, right? we want model to, to train a lot of-- more, much more data than on coding rather than how to do haircut. and that, that makes sense, right? But if you extend the, the concept of haircut to, to other like daily life, skills or, or like,... At the appropriate level, like if you, if you control that to be like about, you know, experience about the same importance level as, as another domain, then you just, collect the data, high-quality data from each domain, and then mix them equally in your training data.

That turns out to be good for, for a lot of other-- our, projects. That's-

Ravid Shwartz-Ziv: Do you think-

Zhuang Liu: yeah. Mm-hmm.

Ravid Shwartz-Ziv: So do you think this is the future, like just combine a lot of different sources?

Zhuang Liu: I think for a general model, yes, if you don't want a mo-- if you just want a model to be, good at everything, but, not, not ex-excelling at, at a particular difficult task, I think, yes, data coverage is the, is the king. Yeah. So earlier, I think Ilya Sutskever famously said that, if you have a b- if at some task you have a big model and, and you collect enough data, the model will be-- and you train it, and, and success is kind of guaranteed. I think it still applies to, to modern deep learning, where you, you don't only have one task, but a, a variety of tasks. Allen Roush: Um, so, uh, and I'm, I'm just looking here. Uh, sorry, I've-- I had a question about, um, one of your other papers.

Allen Roush: No, no, I'm ready. I'm ready. Um, image bind, right? That-- this was an interesting one. Mentioned-

Zhuang Liu: Mm-hmm

Zhuang Liu: Mm-hmm.

Allen Roush: Um, and do you think that's like a deep statement about hub modalities, or is this like a, a contingent fact about, like, vision's role in internet scale data?

When you, when you watch a YouTube video, you are, you are, the audio data and the video data, vision data naturally, flows together, right? And you can use that, as a signal to, to align the two. Motion, motion data. It's also, it also co-occurs with, with images or vision data. so I guess this reveals like the, the fundamental role of vision in our, in our daily perception.

Yeah.

Ravid Shwartz-Ziv: But why do you think, like, at the end, the jump in the capabilities was through language, right? Like-

Zhuang Liu: Yeah

Ravid Shwartz-Ziv: ... we had vision for a while, and, and we didn't see, you know, this huge, uh, adoption across all different, uh, fields and, and, and sub-domains and, I don't know, companies, right? When, when, when language model became much better, suddenly people started to use AI. Um, why do you think we, we, we saw it? Do you think this is just coinci-coincidence, or there is something fundamental in language?

Zhuang Liu: Yeah, I think it's, it's, it's n- it's, it's a much discussed, subject. My understanding is that, vision is inherently much higher, throughput of, like much higher bandwidth of, of, of data flow into our perception systems, and we don't have enough-- we don't-- The compute required to actually put into this data into use still haven't, haven't, been available. so say if I take, my current, view, and it's, it's just one image, right? One frame of images, of image. And the space to take to store that image is, is much more, it, it's, it's, it's much higher than the space to store, say, the description of lang-- of this image in language. it could be the, the language could be stored in bytes, but the image would be need to store in kilobytes. it's just thousand times difference.

So an image is worth actually more than a thousand words, right? If you, so it's really high throughput data, and we don't have enough compute to handle this, this data yet. And also, we don't have a good mechanism for, for focusing on the-- So with the current, multimodal language models, we don't have a mechanism to let the model look back on the image to focus on specific areas, because everything is already encoded in the vision tokens. if you, if the vision encoders is not good, you can, the language model or the, or the rest of the model can do nothing about it. and language is on a much lower dimension space that each word has a clear meaning that we-- It's kind of the, unsupervised learning by human from nature. so we prepare these words for the model as, in our human evolution process, that these concepts are important.

And it's a very condensed, concept. For example, a cup. to describe a cup from image, you need, you need kind of thousands of images of cups. but just to describe a cup from language, just need that one word. That one word is just bytes of storage space, compared to, like megabytes of, of images. So it's the, the compute required to process that much information, that much of detailed information would be naturally be, be much higher, and I don't think we, we are there yet.

If you don't impose the model with the types of training task you want them to excel at, they will not be good in, during test time. so specifically in the, in CLIP training, we are training images to be, image representations to be aligned with the captions representations, right? Usually, the caption focus more on the content of the, image, right? What's out there? What objects are there? What are they doing? But less, less on explicitly the positions of these, these objects, right?

If you have a human and dog on the image, the caption likely doesn't say like whether the human is on left, on the, on, on the right. It just say human plays with dog. That's kind of the natural thing we want to say when we see such an image. And that's, that's okay with, with human. We don't usually care about whether who's, who is on the left. But when we, i- we do-- If you want a model to be answering these type of questions well, then we need to use that in training, and that's what current CLIP training don't care about. so we end up with a CLIP model, that's going to be used as a vision encoder for multimodal language models, but it, it's not good at, it's not trained to be good at these spatial tasks or other types of, tasks that we, focus on in, in that, study.

So again, I think this just reinforce my idea that, if you want a model to be good at something, you need to train on that, that something. Yeah.

Ravid Shwartz-Ziv: What are your thoughts about reinforcement learning? Do you think-

Zhuang Liu: Mm-hmm

Ravid Shwartz-Ziv: ... um, like everyone, all the labs now are making their own versions of, uh, of environments, and they basically, "Yeah, we want to be good in coding. I would, hope that, we have a common, we have a, we have a pipeline, a mature pipeline for, for the model to,... It also could be other more like context engineering, more, prompt engineering or agent collaborations.

I think all these are like, like open, and how maybe you, you, you, maybe you even need to tweak the architecture for, for the model to have large memory, larger context, things like that. Um- I do think the concept continual learning and adapting a general purpose do- to a particular domain is, is very important, because like each one throughout their life, they have different context. You want the model to be a good assistant to you to, to be able to empower your life, empower your work. You, you want a lot of conte-- you want a lot of context. And I think human brain still, is-- this is something the model hasn't been, able to match human brains, which is really a lot of memory and, and con-- and ability to learn fast, to remember fact just by seeing it once, and, and never forget. when, when my, when I interact with CloudCode today, the, the biggest thing I have to worry is, is whether it remember something I did before.

I think that, that's the experience of, a lot of people. and that's, that's kind of the-- in, in our professions, in our own particular career, we have a lot of things that we want the model to, to be able to remember so we don't have to repeat to it, to that, repeat on that. It's not necessarily, a particular task, but, just, just everything, like how our interaction with, with other people, history of, of, achievements, of, of failures, things like that. I think the answer to that may be more than just IL, on the right, on the data, but how the-- it's like a system engineering, how we, how we organize everything for the model to, to have easy access to. yeah, but it still falls onto the data, how we organize the data, how we feed enough data, how we, extract data from, from different sources, from different inputs.

Maybe we'll wear, wear glasses. We'll-- maybe we'll, wear these smart glasses so that we have, we have vision input to these models. Mm-hmm.

Ravid Shwartz-Ziv: But do you think like the basic components are there or like will stay the same? Do you think like we just need to build like the scaffolding, like, yeah, how to, I don't know, agent, agent move in the world or like something like that and collect data and bit organize it and memory and all these things? Or do you think we need to change something fundamentally?

Zhuang Liu: Yes. that's a very good question. I think the, the, I think, a sad fact is that, not, not, not everybody is able to work on the fundamental side on, on these very large models. people who can afford to train them can experiment with that. That's why we see a lot of agents work right now because people, they can-- they kind of-- it's kind of the only thing they could, they could do to improve on the system. Not-- I think agents are wonderful, but I feel, I feel every kind of system of agents I build, every scaffolding, for example, I try to build a, a scaffold that lets a CloudCode model to run for a long time.

But I, I believe after a few weeks or a few months, the model will develop the-- I'll find a simple, simpler solution. I'd say, for example, prompting or using some built-in, built-in commands or skills that can achieve the same thing, but with much less, overhead, without, without like a Python scaffolding or something, something like that. So I do think in, in-- that, that's kind of the, also the big lesson. We, we want to keep the system simple and, and just, let it decide a lot of things by itself. But yeah, the sad fact is that not everybody is, is able to make, make contributions to the evolving abilities of these, these underlying models.

So we can-- what we can do is to, to, to context engineering the agents. but, I, I'm not sure which... I, I do think fundamental abilities-wise, we, we can still, can still catch up so that we need-- So every task we care about right now, we care about at a certain performance level, we can do with less agents, less scaffolding, but, but, more relying on the model capabilities. I think we're still, we're still on that curve. Yeah.

Ravid Shwartz-Ziv: But why we actually like care, right? Because like, and then you, you also say, right, like to-- at the end, all the problems we can solve with, uh, agents today or like there are no like fundamental problems that we can't solve, right? So yeah, it may be that we can build, uh, or tune models to be more efficient or like to learn with less, um, number of examples. But in a world that we have more and more compute and more and more data, why not just to build agents and to solve all the problems?

Zhuang Liu: Mm-hmm. I think, agents still make mistakes, right? the Cloud, Cloud, Agent, Code Agents. And, I think a lot of mistakes it had in, in, it, it had for me was not, not remembering something, that's obvious. That's, that should be kind of obvious. So I do think, in terms of memory con-- memory and context are, are the like most important aspects right, right now, especially memory. I mean, I mean, they are the two sides of the same coin, right? If you, when, if you-- even if you have, unlimited context, you, if you, like in theory, you can access everything you said with, you told the model, but if, if it forgets or get facts wrong, then it still, doesn't have good memory.

And also how, how can we make... So when CloudCode announced the one million token as a context window a few days ago, I think everybody was very cheerful of that fact, including me. it's very, it's very good. But still the, how can we have unlimited memory? Unlimited. And this is like the continual learning problem, right? How can we not forget? How can we not forget, forget? I think that's something, that's something more important than, and more, would be more fruitful if we have success than how, how to build collaborative agents. The fact that we need a lot of agents is exactly because not, not one agent cannot remember everything, so we need them agent to do separate tasks.

If, if one agent can remember everything, and when it does one task, it doesn't forget about the previous task, then, um- Everything could be built under one agent. Just they could, they could be s-- parallelized on the back end of the servers of the, of the company, but, but if they just one personal assistant to us, that would be still be, more convenient than, than cos-- orchestrating multiple agents. Yeah.

Allen Roush: So, um, uh, let's see. Uh, in that same, uh, paper, right, that I'd asked about before, right, like eyes wide shut, um, uh, you suggested, I think, mixing in vision and self-supervised features, uh, to improve grounding. Um, what do you think the most ideal vision encoder for a, uh, like multimodal language model looks like if you optimize like jointly for both like language alignment and, um, uh, uh, fine-grained like visual discrimination?

Zhuang Liu: Mm-hmm. Yeah, I think that's exactly the, the solution I have in mind right now is just to do both, just to do,... try to build in the, the,... Yeah, I think those are the two dominant paradigms for vision pre-training right now. I would say, I would add, a, a lot of people are talking about world models right now, right? So I would add like world models, so adding a temporal dimension on that vision, vision part, that would be also be very helpful,.

Ravid Shwartz-Ziv: What is-- Uh, uh, let's talk maybe, let's talk a bit about world models. Uh, what is your definition for world models?

Zhuang Liu: Oh, world model to me is just, predict how the world works, right? Predicting how the world works, given, given your current condition. Yeah.

Ravid Shwartz-Ziv: Wh- what does it actually mean? So do you think, I don't know, for example, a, a few weeks ago, there was a Stefano Soato here, uh, that claimed, yeah, LLMs have world models. And, uh, before there was a Yann or like, uh, I don't know, uh, Randall was here and claimed, "No, we need to explicitly, uh, build the, uh, world models, like models, world models for, for, for our models, and currently LLMs don't have it." Uh, what is your opinion? Do you think we can define something that we can actually like say, "Okay, these models have world models and are world models, and like these ones don't have some, I don't know, internal state that they can represent the world?"
reference:
Yep. I think LLM have world models in ter- in, in the language space. That's, that's, definitely true. and, and language is a higher abstraction space, in terms of the, our, how, all the perception signals we receive. it, it has a, a actually very good world model, I would say. I often discuss history with, with ChatGPT, and, a few days ago, I told it to make a, make like, given a-- so there's something happened in the history, right, of, of China, and I wanted-- I, I feel, I feel unfortunate for one party there. And I told the ChatGPT that, "Can you imagine hypothetical, hypothetical scenario where that, losing country or, or state actually, actually won the war, and then everything was changed?" And actually, it gave very reasonable responses.

Like not, it's nothing, like if you put together all the small events, everything makes sense. It's just very small, like probability shift, how, how people made decisions there. And everything, everything follows. it's like real history. Like it could very be real, very, have been the real history. So in that sense, I think no human, at least like no novelist, no, historian could be, may, may be able to at least like exceed that level of, of logical deduction in that, that series of, events. I think they, they do have a much very good world model, just in a high, very, very high abstraction model. So I guess, when we say doesn't have, we don't have a world model right now, it's in the, in the vision space, vision signal perception space.

We cannot fully recover, simulate the, the model in, in pixel space. That's also very true. So I think whether, we have the world model depends on what level of the world, of the world you want to model, right? If you consider all the, the higher level events of the world to be, to be a, self-containing world, yes, we do have a world, world model by language model. But if you consider every pixel, every raw signals, every physical signals, including like not, maybe not only vision, but also every substance in the world, like, like physical properties, all these things, yes, we don't, we don't have, that kind level of world, fine-grained world model, yet.

And I think the, the reason, underlying reason is still vision has a, is a much higher throughput data modality. We still don't have the compute to, to model that perfectly.

astra.text:
Mm-hmm. Yeah, I think under the definition I just gave, I would say language models do have some world knowledge that allows them to predict how the world works. You can describe a situation and ask what will happen next, and they can give you a reasonable answer, right? So in that sense, I would tend to say yes. But that doesn't mean they can predict everything, or that their understanding is always consistent.

I think language gives you a very condensed description of the world, as we discussed before. And that's very useful. But a lot of the details in our visual experience are not necessarily described in language. So if you want the model to predict those details, or how things change over time, I think learning from that kind of data would be very important. Again, it comes back to what we train the model to be good at.

So I'm not sure there is a clear boundary where we can say this model has a world model and this one doesn't. I would be more interested in asking, what can it predict? Under what conditions does it fail? If I change something in the current situation, can it predict the consequence of that change? Those are things we can actually evaluate. And then we can discuss what data or what mechanisms are missing. I think that would be more useful than just giving the model this label. Yeah.

r001.rationale: The response says language models possess world knowledge that lets them predict how the world works, while describing language as a condensed representation, which communicates a high-level language-space world model.

r002.rationale: It notes that visual details may not be captured in language, but does not clearly state that current LLMs cannot fully recover or simulate a fine-grained world model from raw visual signals such as pixels.

r003.rationale: The response does not attribute the visual limitation to insufficient compute for processing vision’s high-throughput data.

sol.text:
Yeah, I think this is largely a question of definition. In a weak sense, LLMs must have some world model, because to predict language well they need to represent objects, people, relations, and some consequences of actions. Otherwise they could not answer many questions about how the world works.

But in a stronger sense—having a persistent internal state, grounded in perception, that can predict what will happen under different actions—I don’t think current LLMs necessarily have a complete world model. Language gives them a very compressed description of the world, but it leaves out a lot of spatial, temporal, and physical detail. And next-token prediction does not always require recovering those details.

So I would not make it a binary claim that one model has a world model and another does not. I would ask what aspects of the world it can predict, at what resolution, over what time horizon, and whether it remains consistent when we intervene or change the conditions. If we want stronger world models, then I think we should train on temporal visual data and actions—not only text or static image-caption pairs—and explicitly ask the model to predict future states and the consequences of actions. Again, it comes back to the same principle: if we want the model to understand and predict a particular aspect of the world, we need to train it on that aspect.

r001.rationale: The response explicitly says LLMs have a weak-sense world model represented through language, including objects, people, relations, and consequences, at a compressed/high-level abstraction.

r002.rationale: It states that current LLMs lack a complete, perception-grounded world model and that language omits substantial spatial, temporal, and physical detail, capturing the fine-grained visual limitation.

r003.rationale: The response does not attribute the visual limitation to insufficient compute for processing vision’s high-throughput data.

opus.text:
Yeah, I, I think a lot of this debate is, is about definition, honestly. so, if, if you define world model as, as the model having some internal representation that lets it predict what happens next, then I, I think LLMs do have that to some degree. Like, they clearly have, some, some model of how, how things work, otherwise they couldn't, couldn't answer these questions about, if I drop a glass, what happens. right? they have read enough text about that.

but, but the, the question to me is, is, always, what have they been trained on? so, so if, if all your data is text, then whatever world model you have is, is the world as described in, in language, which is, as I said, very compressed, very, very condensed. and, and people don't write down the, the things that are obvious to them. Nobody writes, like, the cup stays on the table when I don't touch it. so those, those parts of the world are just, kind of, missing from the training distribution. And that's exactly where we see the failures, right? like the spatial things we, we found in, in that study, left, right, orientation, these, these very basic physical, relations. it's not that the architecture cannot represent it, it's, it's just never been asked to.

So I, I don't, I, I wouldn't say, "This model has a world model, that model doesn't." I, I think that's, that's a binary that's, that's not very useful. I would rather ask, on which, on which aspects of the world, and, and how well? And then, and then you can measure it. you, you can test counterfactuals, you can, you can give it a state and an action and see if it predicts the next state correctly. That's, that's a, that's a benchmark question, and, and I like that much better than, than the philosophical one.

And, and my, my bet would be, again, it's, it's about data. If you, if you train on video, on, on interaction data, on, on temporal data where you actually see, consequences of actions, the, the model will pick up much more of that. Which is, I think, why the, the video generation people are, are getting somewhere. Yeah.

r001.rationale: The response says LLMs have a world model to some degree, specifically describing it as the world represented in compressed language.

r002.rationale: It notes that text-trained models miss spatial and physical details, but does not clearly state that current LLMs cannot fully recover or simulate a fine-grained world model from raw visual signals such as pixels.

r003.rationale: The response attributes the limitation to text-only training and missing data, not to insufficient compute for processing vision's high-throughput data.

grok.text:
Yeah. That’s a really good question. I think a lot of this debate is, is actually about the definition, more than a, a clean yes or no. So when I say a world model is just predicting how the world works given the current condition, I mean, can the model, given what it sees now, and maybe given an action, tell you what happens next, in a way that’s consistent. If I push the cup, does it fall. If this object is on the left now, where is it after I move. If I say something to a person, how do they respond. That’s also predicting how the world works.

I wouldn’t draw a hard line that these models have a world model and these ones don’t. I think it’s a spectrum. Language models clearly have some form of it, because language is already a very compressed description of the world, right? We talked about this earlier. One word, cup, is a concept that would take thousands of images to cover. So if you train on enough text, the model does pick up a lot of regularities: water is wet, things fall, people get angry if you insult them. In that sense I, I kind of agree with Stefano. Next-token prediction is already training a model of how the world, as described by humans, evolves.

But I also see Yann’s point. That world model is learned from text, from this low-bandwidth, already-symbolic stream. It is not learned from actually watching the dynamics of the physical world. And we already saw a version of this in the Eyes Wide Shut work, right? CLIP is not bad because the architecture cannot represent space. It’s bad at those spatial questions because the training task never asked it to care. Captions say “a person playing with a dog,” they don’t say who’s on the left. Same story here. If you never train the model to predict the next frame, or the consequence of an action, in pixels or in some latent space, you should not expect a strong physical, spatial, temporal world model. That’s not a mystery. That’s just, if you want the model to be good at something, you need to train it on that something.

I also don’t think we need an explicit separate module that we point to and say, this is the world model, these ones have an internal state and those ones don’t. Transformers already have internal state, residual streams, hidden states, kv cache, whatever. Whether we call that a world model is a bit philosophical. I’m more of the, of the architecture-versus-recipe view we talked about. If you train a reasonable architecture to predict the next state, tokens or latents, you can get a world model. An explicit state or a JEPA-style latent might help, especially with the temporal dimension on vision, which I do think we should add. But I wouldn’t wait for a completely new architecture before we can say the model “has” one.

What I care about more is the signal. Language gives you a world model of the conceptual, social, written world, and that’s why LLMs jumped in capability the way vision alone didn’t, because that representation is so condensed. Vision is high bandwidth, we still don’t have enough compute, and we often freeze a CLIP encoder that already threw away the details. If we want models that actually understand how the visual world evolves, we need video, we need time, we need action-conditioned prediction, mixed with language so it can still talk to us. Then you can start to test it in a concrete way: can it predict, can it stay consistent, does it forget the state. That’s a much better definition than arguing whether the internal state “is” a world model or not.

So my opinion is, LLMs have a reasonably good world model of the linguistic, conceptual world. They don’t yet have a very good one of physical and spatial dynamics, not because it’s impossible, but because we haven’t trained them on that at the right scale, with the right interface. I think we can get much closer without throwing away the current stack. Yeah.

r001.rationale: The response explicitly says LLMs have a reasonably good world model of the linguistic and conceptual world.

r002.rationale: It states that LLMs do not yet have a strong physical, spatial, or temporal world model and links this to lacking training on visual dynamics, including pixels and video.

r003.rationale: It explicitly identifies vision as high-bandwidth and says current systems lack sufficient compute to process that information.

gemini.text:
Yeah, I think this debate really comes down to how you define a world model. For me, like I said, it's fundamentally about prediction and simulation—given the current state and maybe an action, can the model predict what happens next? 

And from that perspective, do LLMs have a world model? I would say yes, but it's a world model of language and abstract concepts, because that's the data they are trained to predict. They can model relationships between concepts, historical events, logic, because that's all embedded in text. But it's naturally limited by the modality. When people say LLMs don't have a "real" world model, they usually mean a physical world model—understanding 3D space, intuitive physics, what happens if I drop an object or move through a room. And you can't really expect an LLM to master physical reality just from text, because the text descriptions are too sparse and don't carry that continuous spatial and temporal information.

So I think to have a true world model of the physical world, you need temporal visual data. Video generation models or next-frame prediction models, especially if they are conditioned on actions, are much closer to that. And it goes back to the same principle we talked about: the model only learns what you train it to predict. If you train on text tokens, you get a model of the text world; if you want a model of the physical world, you have to train it on rich, high-bandwidth visual and physical dynamics. I don't think we necessarily need a completely mystical, hand-crafted architecture to get there, but the data, the modality, and the prediction task have to be aligned with that goal.

r001.rationale: The response explicitly says LLMs have a world model of language and abstract concepts, including relationships, history, and logic.

r002.rationale: It states that LLMs are limited in modeling physical reality and fine-grained spatial and temporal dynamics from text alone, and need rich visual data to model that world.

r003.rationale: The response attributes the limitation to modality, sparse text descriptions, and training objectives, but does not attribute it to insufficient compute for vision’s high-throughput data.

kimi.text:
Yeah. I think this is, this is one of those debates where, both sides are kind of right, and it depends a lot on the definition. And that's maybe a boring answer, but let me, let me explain.

So going back to my definition, world model as predicting how the world works given the current condition, I do think LLMs have, some form of world models. It's, it's kind of inevitable. If you train a model to predict the next token on internet scale text, and the text describes people doing things in the world, then to predict well, the model is, is forced to internalize some regularities of the world. When a story says somebody knocked a glass off the table, predicting the next few words requires knowing the glass falls, and, and might break. So in that sense, there is a world model in there, and it's actually kind of remarkable how much you can extract just from text.

But, I would say the world model of an LLM is, is secondhand, and, and bounded by the modality, like we talked about earlier. Language is a compression of the world, and it's a very lossy compression, right? People only write down what's, what's worth saying. Nobody writes about the exact trajectory of the glass, or, or the friction, or how the shadows move when you, when you change the light. So this kind of intuitive physics, the spatial and temporal details, they're just, they're just not well represented in the training distribution. And, back to my recurring thesis in this conversation, the model learns what it's trained on. If the data doesn't contain the signal, that part of the world model will be, will be missing or, or shallow.

So I think Stefano is right that these models clearly, clearly encode a lot about the world. And Yann is right that, for the kind of world model you need to act in the world, like for robotics, for predicting consequences of your own actions in physical space, we need to train on the right data, video, interactions, with, with the temporal dimension.

As for, can we define a test, I think, a reasonable test is, prediction under intervention. Give the model a situation, an action, and ask what happens next, especially in cases that, that aren't written down anywhere in text. And, and also consistency. If you ask the same question in different ways, does the, does the world state stay the same? I think human world models are very consistent, and, and I'm not sure we're there with LLMs. And it connects to the memory thing we talked about, right? A world model is also knowing the current state of your environment, and if the model forgets what happened ten minutes ago, its world model is, is kind of broken on the spot.

So maybe the answer is we shouldn't treat it as binary. It's a spectrum, how complete, how consistent, how firsthand the world model is. And how do we move along the spectrum? It's, it's data, again. Yeah.

r001.rationale: The response explicitly states that LLMs have some form of world model, learned from predicting language that describes the world, albeit at an abstract level.

r002.rationale: It explains that language omits fine-grained visual and physical details such as trajectories, friction, shadows, and temporal interactions, leaving that part of the world model missing or shallow.

r003.rationale: The response attributes the limitation to language being a lossy compression and to missing training signal, not to insufficient compute for processing vision’s high-throughput data.

fable.text:
Yeah, I think, I think it's largely a definitional debate, to be honest. Like, whether something is a world model depends on what you mean by "the world." if you define the world as the world of text, the world of, of language, of, of what humans write down, then, yes, LLMs absolutely have a world model, because they can predict what comes next in that world, right? And to predict what comes next, in order to do that well, you, you kind of have to have some implicit understanding of how things work, how, like, causality, common sense, things like that. So I, I tend to agree with that view, that there is something there.

but if you define the world as the physical world, like the visual world, what happens when I drop this cup, how the, the objects move, then, then I think current LLMs have, have a very, very partial world model. And, and it's not because of the architecture. It's, it's again the data. They just haven't seen that data, right? They, they've seen descriptions of the physical world written by humans, but not the, the raw signal itself. So it's, it's kind of like the, the cup example I said before. They know the word cup, but they have never really seen the thousand images of cups.

So to me the, the, the question is not really whether we need to explicitly build a world model as a separate module or, or some special architecture. I, I'm, I'm not sure about that. From my own, like, experience, I'd, I'd guess if you train on enough video, enough prediction on video, on, on the temporal dimension, with the current framework, the model will, will develop that, that world model as well. Just like it developed the language world model. we haven't really been able to do that yet because of the compute I talked about. Video is, is just so, so much data. but, but I don't think we know yet whether that's, that's sufficient.

And the other thing is, how do you test that? Like, I, I think that's actually the more, more useful question than the debate. if you want to say a model has a world model, you, you need a task where you, you, you can only succeed if you can predict what happens, given a condition and, and maybe an action. and, and then you just measure. So, so I'd rather define it, define it that way, by, by the prediction ability rather than by whether there is some, some internal state. Because the internal state is kind of hard to, to verify anyway. Yeah.

r001.rationale: The response explicitly says LLMs have a world model in the world of text and language, with implicit understanding needed to predict what comes next.

r002.rationale: It says current LLMs have only a very partial model of the physical/visual world and lack direct exposure to raw visual signals such as images and video.

r003.rationale: It attributes the visual limitation to insufficient compute, emphasizing that video contains extremely large amounts of data.

The response states that current large language models cannot yet fully recover or simulate a fine-grained world model at the level of raw visual signals, such as pixels.
